en: Preface to the *Record of Auspicious Responses to Rebirth in the Western Pure Land* Now, while the Buddhas give rise to compassion through manifold skillful means, rebirth in the Western Land is the single path most easily in accord with the capacities and conditions of sentient beings.

Examining the sincere aspirations of those in antiquity, it is evident that they all experienced spiritual resonance with auspicious signs. Thus, there was the Venerable Master Sha... [text continues]
The monk Wen-shen of Men-chen recorded the śrāmaṇera Xiao Kang in the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks),
extolling his true virtues within the context of the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth).
Preface: Recording the rare and marvelous,
attesting to the conditions for sincere devotion and transformative influence,
and manifesting the inconceivable efficacy of the Buddha’s power.
Thus, it ensured that the Way would not fall into decline across the ages, causing both monastics and laypeople to turn their hearts toward it;
the profound wind was renewed once more,
and a magnificent undertaking was restored.
This is intended to cause those who have resolved their minds to become firm and free from doubt,
and to provide a path for those who have not yet given rise to faith to rely upon.
I have merely set forth this preface for that purpose.
1. Dharma Master Huiyuan. First: Dharma Master Huiyuan was a monk of the Eastern Jin dynasty.
He was a native of Yanmen and chose to reside on Mount Lu.
For more than thirty years,
his shadow did not leave the mountains,
and his traces did not enter the secular world.
He saw guests off with the Tiger Brook as the boundary.
Although he was broadly versed in the various classics,
he was particularly devoted to the Western [Dharma].
A Pure Land Hall was established beneath the cliffs,
where morning and evening rites and repentances were performed.
Among those who attended were the courtier Xie Lingyun and the eminent recluse Liu Yimin.
Together they renounced worldly glory and jointly cultivated the Pure Land;
there were one hundred and twenty-three lay devotees in total.
Before the image of Amitāyus,
he established a fast and made a vow;
he left behind a written composition in praise and eulogy.
He had a vision of an immortal riding upon clouds while listening to the teachings,
or perhaps chanting pure hymns as he rode the long wind.
On the sixth day of the eighth month in the twelfth year of the Yixi era, the Dharma Master—
The noble assembly welcomed him from afar;
at the time of his passing, he entrusted [the teachings] and entered parinirvāṇa lying on his right side.
He was eighty-three years old. 2.
Dharma Master Tanluan: Regarding Dharma Master Tanluan of the Qi Dynasty, his family resided near Mount Wutai.
He possessed a profound and thorough understanding of all the Buddhist teachings.
Having obtained ten fascicles of the *Xiānjīng* (Scripture of the Immortals) from this land,
he wished to visit Tao Yinyu to study the arts of immortality.
Later, he encountered a Tripiṭaka Bodhisattva, who asked him:
"Within the Buddha-dharma, is there a method for longevity and immortality that surpasses the *xián jīng* (immortal scriptures) of this land?
The Tripitaka Master spat on the ground and said in alarm,
"Where in this region is there any such method for longevity and immortality?"
Even if one attains an extended lifespan,
when the years are exhausted,
one must fall [into the lower realms]. He then bestowed the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* upon Zhilun, saying:
This is the method of the Great Sage;
practice it accordingly,
and you shall long attain liberation.
He was to be forever free from birth and death.
Luan then required fire and proceeded to burn the immortal scriptures.
Suddenly, in the middle of the night, he saw a Brahman monk enter his room.
He said to Luan,
"I am the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna," and then he spoke this verse:
Leaves that have already fallen cannot be reattached to the branches;
millet for the future cannot be sought within the granary;
a white horse passing through a crevice cannot be made to pause even for a moment.
That which has already passed cannot be returned; that which is yet to come cannot be pursued.
Where does the present dwell? Like a white colt, it is difficult to turn back.
Only the Dharma Master knows that his life has reached its end.
He gathered more than three hundred disciples;
holding a censer himself and facing west,
he instructed his followers and exhorted them to revere the Western Land.
At the moment the sun first rises,
they shall recite the Buddha's name in unison;
then, their lives will immediately come to an end.
Five *li* to the west of the temple was a convent for nuns.
One heard the sound of celestial music coming from the west and going to the east;
after a short while, it was heard again coming from the east and going to the west.

3. Chan Master Daozhen. Regarding Chan Master Daozhen of the Liang Dynasty, the third [section]: While practicing the recitation of the Buddha's name at Mount Lu, Master Daozhen cultivated the visualization of water (*āp-kasiṇa*).
Consequently, he dreamed of water.
A hundred people were traveling by boat toward the West;
they sought to be taken along for a ride,
but the people on board would not allow it.
Zheng said, "I,
this poor monk, have spent my entire life cultivating the practices for the Western Paradise.
Why do you not allow me to go?"
A person on the boat said,
"Your practice is not yet perfected;
you have not yet recited the Amitābha Sūtra."
They also prepared a bathhouse,
and thus the boatmen set sail all at once;
yet Zhen was unable to go.
He woke from his weeping and recited sutras and bathed the monks.
After a long time, he dreamed again.
A person riding upon a white silver pavilion raised his hand and said,
"Venerable Master Chen!"
Your karma is already complete;
you may now employ your mind as you wish.
Therefore, I have come to inform you.
He was destined for rebirth in the Western Pure Land.
On the night of his passing,
thousands of torches appeared as if arrayed upon the mountain peak.
A rare fragrance filled the temple.
Later, from within the scripture case, he recovered the "Record Left for His Living Disciples," which he had not disclosed to anyone prior to his passing.
4. Sengyai. Sengyai was the fourth [patriarch] during the Later Zhou dynasty. He resided at Duobao Monastery in Yizhou.
By nature, he spoke little and did not engage in frivolous play.
Whenever he traveled through mountain forests,
he would remain there for the entire day.
When people asked him why, [he replied:]
He replied,
"The person is indeed loathsome;
I am merely contemplating it."
To the west of the city, he burned off the five fingers of his left hand.
Hundreds of thousands of monastics and laypeople crowded around him, weeping.
The Master said:
I merely maintain the bodhisattva mind;
I do not weep. When people ask whether it is painful, [I say: "It is."
He replied:
"Since the mind has no pain,
what do you point to as being painful?"
His palms were burned by fire and his marrow boiled and surged forth.
When people asked him the reason for this, he replied:
The answer is:
It is because sentient beings are unable to practice patience.
Now, observe that those who lack patience are burned, whereas those who possess patience are not burned.
He further addressed the assembly, saying:
"In the final age, people will be arrogant, frivolous, and shallow;
they will look upon a Buddha image and see nothing but a piece of wood."
Hearing the sutras was like the wind passing over a horse's ears;
he burned his hand and destroyed his body out of a desire to inspire faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma.
He said to his disciples:
"After my parinirvāṇa,
you should diligently make offerings to the sick, the ugly, and even to animals."
Most of those who belong to such groups are manifestations of the skillful means of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Were it not for a great mind of equanimity,
how could one show reverence toward all?
In some instances, he saw celestial flowers and the mountain cliffs;
clad in a variegated *kāṣāya* and holding a mendicant’s staff,
he was accompanied by six hundred monks.
He ascended into the air and vanished toward the west.
5. Chan Master Huiming. Chan Master Huiming, the fifth [entry], was a native of Taiyuan during the Later Zhou dynasty.
He was a spiritual friend to Chan Master Huisi of Mount Nanyue.
While performing the Vaipulya repentance ritual,
he looked at him from beneath the pine trees and wept, saying,
"In these two places alone, one may bring one's life to its end."
Before ten days had passed, he was stricken by illness;
sitting in the full lotus posture facing west,
he cried out, "The Buddha is coming!"
They passed away with their palms joined;
both were eighty-three years old.
At that time, people saw them in dreams.
Devas and humans raised banners and streamers,
crying out, "Excellent!
Come to welcome the two masters as they depart."

6. Chan Master Jing’ai. Regarding Chan Master Jing’ai of the sixth [section], during his time as a layman in the Later Zhou dynasty, he entered a temple and beheld the transformation tableaux of the hells.
He said to his peers,
"Examine karma as it truly is;
who can escape this suffering?"
He then informed his mother and left the household life.
He resided constantly in forests and wild places.
The community of monks asked him:
"The Master ought to remain in the world to guide and transform others,
yet he has instead lost himself in the forests and springs. Ai said:
The Way values practice and application;
it does not reside in anything else.
One observes the timing to advance or retreat.
Furthermore, he lived in seclusion.
During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou dynasty, when the Buddha-dharma was suppressed,
Seng’ai lamented that he lacked the power to protect the Dharma.
He addressed his disciples, saying:
"I have brought no benefit to the world;
I shall now relinquish my own body."
He sat cross-legged upon a rock,
spread out his patched robe,
and then cut it himself.
He cut his hands and feet into pieces and spread them upon the rocks;
he drew out his intestines and entrails and hung them from the branches of trees;
furthermore, he used a knife to cut out his heart.
He passed away while holding it.
His final letter stated:
"To all those with whom there is a karmic affinity..."
Within the Buddha-dharma,
do not give rise to regression;
you must certainly support and promote wholesome benefits.
There are five reasons for relinquishing this body and life based on three conditions.
First, seeing many faults within oneself.
Second, being unable to protect the Dharma.
Third, desiring to see the Buddha quickly,
he then recited a verse, saying:
"May all sentient beings..."
Hearing that I have relinquished my body,
you have perfected the divine ear and reached the ultimate realization of bodhi.
This body is a vessel of impurity;
it is a sack of excrement below,
with nine orifices from which things flow out.
Like a full embankment or pond,
one casts off this defiled body,
vowing to be reborn in the Pure Land.
In a single thought, the flower blossomed at the abode of Amitābha Buddha. 7.
Dhyāna Master Yi. Dhyāna Master Yi, the seventh [entry], was the Tiantai Dhyāna Master Yi of the Sui dynasty. He was a native of Yingchuan.
While Chen Dai was lecturing on the Vimalakīrti Sūtra,
he suddenly saw three jeweled stairways descend from the sky,
with dozens of Brahma-monks holding censers.
He entered the hall and circumambulated Zhiyi three times;
Zhiyi then said,
"Since my birth..."
Sit facing the west and recite the names of Amitābha Buddha, Mahāprajñā, Avalokiteśvara, and Śrīghoṣa;
the power of their majestic spiritual authority does not exceed this.
I have frequently performed the Avalokiteśvara Repentance.
Since falling ill,
my mindfulness of the Western Land has become increasingly earnest.
"I should go with you.
There was someone bringing medicine,
who replied:
The illness does not unite with the body;
old age does not unite with the mind.
How, then, could medicine possibly dispel the illness?
My life was a weary vessel of poison;
in death, I am liberated and return to rest.
Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta have now come to welcome me.
Instruct them to chant the title of the Lotus Sūtra,
and praise it, saying:
"The father and mother of all Dharma-gates."
Wisdom and understanding arise therefrom;
subtle and profound, it is difficult to fathom,
and today it has been severed.
Furthermore, they chanted the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* and praised it, saying:
"The forty-eight vows."
The pure land is adorned with lotus ponds and jewel trees;
though it is easy to reach, no one goes there.
He further commanded the *karmadāna*, saying,
"Upon hearing the bell at the moment of death,
one's right mindfulness shall increase."
"Moreover, each of you remain silent.
I shall now depart.
Having finished speaking, he passed away.
He was sixty years old.
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, he passed away.
He had constructed forty-five temples.
He ordained four thousand monks,
transcribed fifteen sets of the Buddhist canon,
and fashioned more than one hundred thousand images of gold, silver, and sandalwood.
He was none other than the Great Master Zhizhe Fashang.
8. Sengdaoyu, the Eighth: During the Sui Dynasty, the monk Sengdaoyu recited the name of Amitābha Buddha at Kaijue Temple.
He fashioned a sandalwood image three inches tall.
Later, Daoyu suddenly died;
after seven days, he revived and said:
First, he saw a virtuous person being reborn at the edge of a precious pond.
As the person circumambulated the flowers three times,
the flowers immediately blossomed.
He then entered and sat down;
he circumambulated the flower three times,
yet the flower did not open.
He brushed away the flowers with his hand,
and the flowers withered and fell away accordingly.
Amitābha Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"You should first return to that country,
repent for all your transgressions,
and bathe yourself with fragrant water."
"When the morning star appears,
I shall come to welcome you;
you must create an image of me."
"For what reason is it so small?
Upāli replied,
"If the mind is great, it is great."
"If one's mind is small, the image is small.
Having finished speaking, the image filled the entirety of space.
Thereupon, he bathed it with fragrant water.
With single-mindedness,
he repented and addressed the assembly, saying,
"I shall use an analogy to illustrate the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha."
When the morning star appeared,
transformation Buddhas came to welcome him;
all those present beheld his radiance and heard it.
Even after his life had ended, it was the eighth year of the Kaihuang era. 9.
Dharma Master Deng: During the Sui dynasty, Dharma Master Deng lectured on the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* at Xingguo Monastery in Bingzhou.
Monastics and laypeople came to listen;
whether old or young,
they were orally instructed in the name of Amitābha Buddha.
She exhorted others to be reborn together [in the Pure Land].
In the twelfth year of the Kaihuang era,
a rare fragrance came to welcome her.
On the day of the funeral procession, clouds of incense pervaded all the villages. 10.
Dharma Master Hong: Dharma Master Hong of the Sui dynasty was a native of Bingzhou.
Throughout his life, he practiced with diligence, refrained from grasping at money or treasures,
constantly kept the Western Quarter in mind,
and aspired for Amitābha Buddha.
At the time of his death,
he saw the boys and girls of Tuṣita Heaven coming to welcome him.
The Dharma Master said:
I aspire for the Western Land and shall not be reborn in the heavens;
I cause my followers to practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
She said, "The Buddha from the West has come to welcome me.
Having spoken these words, she passed away;
this was in the fourth year of the Renshou era.
11. Meditation Master Daochuo. Meditation Master Daochuo, the eleventh [patriarch], was a native of Bingzhou during the Tang Dynasty.
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* two hundred times at Xuanzhong Temple.
For seven years, he practiced samādhi and mastered the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
he personally drilled the beads of his rosary and exhorted others to recite the Buddha’s name.
He always spoke with a smile.
Once, while facing west, he said to Shandao,
"I fear that Daochuo will not attain rebirth."
"Venerable Master, would it be possible for you to enter meditative concentration so that we may see the Buddha?
The Skillful Guide entered concentration and saw the Buddha at a height of over one hundred chi, saying:
Daochuo was currently practicing the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation,
yet he did not know whether he would be able to cast off this retribution-body to attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
He asked again:
"In what month and year was he born?
He replied:
"As one fells a tree, the axe falls continuously."
Do not speak with those who have no affinity;
upon returning home, do not complain of hardship.
Furthermore, command Chuo to perform repentance.
First, to leave the scriptures and images in a shallow place while residing oneself in a secure room;
second, to perform meritorious deeds on behalf of those who have left the household life.
Third, one should repent before the Sangha of the ten directions for any injury caused to living beings during the construction and repair [of monasteries].
One should repent before all sentient beings.
He asked again,
"At the time of death, what auspicious signs will appear for people to see and hear?
He replied:
On the day of my passing, I shall emit light from my white tuft,
shining far toward the east;
when this light appears, [it shall be so].
He will come to be born in my land.
Indeed, on the day of his passing,
three rays of light from his white hair-ūrṇā illuminated the interior of the room.
Furthermore, he saw the light of Dharma Master Tanyuan within a pond of the seven treasures, who said:
"The Pure Land has already been realized."
As his residual karmic retribution was not yet exhausted, he appeared three times over the realm of the purple clouds. 12.
Chan Master Shandao. Chan Master Shandao, the twelfth [patriarch], was surnamed Zhu and was a Chan master of the Tang Dynasty.
He was a native of Sizhou.
Having left home to become a monk in his youth,
he once saw a transformation tableau of the Western Paradise and sighed, saying:
When shall we entrust our physical forms to the lotus pedestal and settle our spirits in the Pure Land?
Upon receiving full ordination,
he and the Venerable Miaokai examined the *Amitābha Sūtra* together.
Hearing this, he sighed with joy and said:
"Cultivating other practices leads to deviations and is difficult to perfect;
only this gate of contemplation can certainly transcend birth and death."
He then went to the Venerable Master Chao and asked,
"Is it truly possible to attain rebirth through the practice of nianfo?
The Master replied:
Each person shall prepare a single lotus flower.
If it does not wither after seven days of walking the path, one will attain rebirth there.
Furthermore, Dharma Master Ying of the Eastern Capital lectured on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra forty times.
He entered the meditation hall of Master Chuo and,
while roaming in samādhi, sighed and said:
"I have regretted for many years that I have merely exhausted my body and mind in vainly searching through literary commentaries.
Who would have expected that the practice of Buddha-recitation is so inconceivable?
The Zen Master said:
The sutras contain sincere words;
how could the Buddha speak falsely?
Throughout his life, the Meditation Master always delighted in begging for food.
He reproached himself every day, saying:
"Even Śākyamuni went out to beg for alms;
what kind of person am I, Shandao, to sit idly at home awaiting offerings?"
He did not even accept prostrations from śrāmaṇeras.
He transcribed one hundred thousand scrolls of the Amitābha Sūtra and painted two hundred sets of illustrations depicting the Transformation Scenes of the Pure Land.
Every stupa and temple he saw was restored and maintained.
Since the Buddha-dharma traveled eastward,
there has never been such a flourishing of Chan masters.
13. Dharma Master Xuan. Dharma Master Xuan of the Tang Dynasty was a native of Bingzhou.
It was only upon encountering Meditation Master Chao lecturing on the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra* that he first turned his mind toward the Dharma.
For five years he specialized in the recitation of the Buddha’s name;
for one day and one night, he performed a thousand prostrations and recited the Buddha’s name seventy thousand times.
Fearing the end of his life, he redoubled his diligent practice.
He dreamed that Śākyamuni Buddha and Mañjuśrī praised the Lotus Sūtra;
he also dreamed of three paths leading toward the west.
The first path is always for laypeople;
the second path comprises both monastics and laity;
the third path consists exclusively of the Sangha.
The Master said: "These are all people who have attained rebirth.
**Master An, the Fourteenth:** Master An of the Tang Dynasty was a native of Bingzhou.
He cultivated the practices for rebirth in the Pure Land.
Every time he performed the Vaipulya repentance,
at the moment of his death,
the two Bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta appeared in the air before him.
He summoned the court painters,
but none were able to paint it.
Suddenly, he was moved by two men who said:
Having come from the Western Capital,
he intended to go to Mount Tai;
he then completed the illustrations for him.
He vanished without a trace.
The Master said to his disciples,
"Who among you can follow me to the West?"
The youngest boy said,
"I wish to follow you," and immediately entered the ritual arena, where he sat upright and passed away.
He was eighty years of age.
On the seventh day of the first month in the first year of the Chuigong era, he passed away.
15. Chan Master Daxing. Chan Master Daxing, the fifteenth, was a native of Qizhou.
He entered Mount Tai, clothing himself in grass and subsisting on wood,
seeking the Samādhi of the Lotus Sūtra;
he was moved by the manifestation of the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra before his eyes.
The teacher recited the name of Amitābha Buddha for twenty-one days.
When it was nearly midnight,
Suddenly he saw a ground of lapis lazuli;
his mind’s eye was brilliantly clear, perceiving the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Afterwards, he passed away quickly, reclining on his right side.
After the burial, a strange fragrance emanated from the inner and outer coffins for several days without dispersing;
his countenance remained as if he were alive, with no difference at all.
16. Chan Master Zang. Chan Master Zang was a native of Fenzhou.
Upon leaving the gate, he visited all the stupas and temples.
He did not accept the prostrations of the secular way, rising before others to restrain his mind and halt the six thieves.
With a single thought of awakening, he was free from error.
Whenever there were matters concerning the Sangha,
he took the place of servants;
seeing their soiled robes, he would secretly collect, wash, and mend them.
In the height of summer, he would strip off his clothes and enter the grass to feed the mosquitoes and gadflies.
On the day of his death,
the various devas came in succession to invite him, yet he would not go.
Only when the transformation Buddhas come to welcome him in the Pure Land does he finally depart. 17.
On the Reverend Gan: The Reverend Gan resided at Qianfu Monastery in Chang’an.
He was extensively versed in the classics but did not believe in the practice of Buddha-recitation.
He asked Master Shandao:
Regarding the question of how the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) is performed,
the answer is:
"If you can single-mindedly recite the Buddha's name."
"You shall realize it for yourself.
He asked again,
"Have you seen the Buddha?"
The Master said,
"How can one doubt the words of the Buddha? Thereupon,
he entered the meditation hall for twenty-one days, yet no response occurred.
Regretting his own deep transgressions, he resolved to fast until death;
however, his teacher stopped him and would not permit it.
For three years, he remained single-minded in his devotion.
He subsequently beheld the Buddha’s golden body and the white tuft of hair between his eyebrows,
and attained samādhi;
he then composed the *Wǎngshēng Juéyì Lùn* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts Concerning Rebirth) in seven fascicles.
At the time of death, the Buddha comes to welcome him;
he joins his palms as he comes from the west, or he passes away facing west.
18. Chan Master Huaiyu. Chan Master Huaiyu, the eighteenth, was surnamed Gao.
He resided at Yongquan Temple in Taizhou;
he did not eat food grown by his own household,
nor did he wear silk from silkworms.
He constantly performed repentance for his own karma more than ten million times.
He recited the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Contemplation Sūtra* three hundred thousand times and daily chanted the names of the Buddhas fifty thousand times.
He released lice and fleas back into nature and remained seated for long periods without lying down.
On the ninth day of the sixth month in the sixth year of the Tiānbǎo era.
He saw a multitude of holy beings from the West, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
He saw one person carrying a white silver platform, entering through a window.
The Chan Master said:
"Through my daily devotions, I have obtained a golden platform," he said,
and so he redoubled his efforts in the practice of nianfo.
Then, a voice from the air proclaimed:
A halo of light circled his crown,
its radiance pervading all of space.
He spoke to his disciples, saying:
Do not allow them to touch the light after they have retreated.
At the time of death,
the color and brilliance of the light will become even more intense.
Then he spoke in verse:
Pure and radiant, free from dust and defilement, I was born by transformation from a lotus as my parents.
Having practiced the path for ten kalpas, I have appeared in Jambudvīpa to undergo various sufferings.
Having practiced asceticism throughout his life for more than ten kalpas, he forever left the Sahā world to return to the Pure Land.
After reciting these verses, he beheld a purple-golden platform and passed away with a smile.
His physical body remains present at Yongquan Temple in Taizhou.
19. Sengfazhi. Sengfazhi, the nineteenth [patriarch], resided at Tiantai. He took the practice of mindfulness of the Buddha as his vocation.
By nature, he was somewhat coarse and impetuous.
He did not observe the monastic discipline.
People often said of him,
"He has committed a *duṣkṛta* offense."
At nine hundred years of age, he entered hell.
Immediately upon hearing the sutra and with faith reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha once, he extinguished the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.
Thereupon, at Guoqing Temple’s Tuṣita Terrace, he recited the Buddha’s name day and night.
The people of the time did not believe him.
Suddenly, he took leave of both the monastics and the laity, saying,
"I wish to be reborn in the Pure Land."
She instructed her relatives and acquaintances to prepare a one-day vegetarian feast.
At midday on that day,
she passed away without illness.
A golden light shone for several hundred li.
Wild pheasants cried out in alarm,
and the boatmen upon the river thought it was dawn.
20. Sengda’ang, Sengda’ang. Regarding the twentieth, Sengda’ang, while he was lecturing on the Lotus Sutra in Xiangzhou, he suddenly saw a multitude of musical instruments descending from the sky.
Because he had informed the Tuṣita Heaven, they came down to welcome him.
Daowang said,
"The heavenly realm is the very root of birth and death."
"I have never wished for anything else;
my thoughts have been fixed solely upon the Western Quarter.
As soon as he finished speaking, he saw celestial music and dancers turning in a circle to come and welcome him.
"The messenger has arrived; you must not remain for long.
Having finished speaking, he took the incense burner in his hand and, sitting upright upon his high seat, passed away suddenly.
21. Sengxiongjun (Sengxiongjun), the twenty-first: Sengxiongjun’s secular surname was Zhou.
He was a native of Chengdu.
He was skilled at lecturing and preaching, yet lacked moral discipline.
They misappropriated the offerings and gains they received for unrighteous purposes;
furthermore, they returned to lay life to join military camps and engage in slaughter,
or fled from hardships only to re-enter the monastic community.
During the Dali era,
he saw himself being judged for entry into hell by King Yama.
Jun cried out in a loud voice:
"If the heroic and eminent one were to enter hell,
then the Buddhas of the three periods would be speaking falsehoods.
The King said:
The Buddha never speaks falsely.
Jun said:
"Observe the 'Lower Grade, Lower Birth' section of the *Amitābha Sūtra*."
Even those who have committed the five heinous crimes attain rebirth in the Pure Land through ten recitations at the moment of death;
although Jun has committed sins,
he has not perpetrated the five heinous crimes.
As for those who practiced mindfulness of the Buddha,
their number is beyond reckoning;
as soon as they finished speaking, they were reborn in the Western Pure Land.
She departed by ascending the platform. 22.
Bhikṣuṇī Fǎzàng: Second Part. During the Song Dynasty, Bhikṣuṇī Fǎzàng resided at Jiànfú Monastery in Jīnlíng.
His practice of dhyāna was lofty and far-reaching.
He said to his fellow student Tanjing,
"In establishing my person and practicing the Way, I have followed [his example]."
His aspirations were set upon the Western Land.
Later, he suddenly fell ill;

This *Account of Auspicious Responses of Rebirth in the Western Pure Land* was transcribed by the śramaṇa Jien of Enryaku-ji, who had crossed the sea, on the twenty-ninth day of the fourth month in the second year of the Ten-toku era (the year of Wumu, 948 CE), a Gengchen day, a Thursday, under the Zuī lunar mansion. It was recorded as a transmission based on the oral instructions of the Grand Master Huiguang, who was granted the purple robe by the Great Tang state of Wuyue.

The manuscript transmitted over the years was lost in the fire of the first year of Hoan-ten (1139). On the ninth day of the ninth month of the second year of Kōji (1145), it was ordered that this be rewritten. (In red ink: The punctuation was adjusted and a comparison was made. On the third day of the third month of the third year of Ōan (1370), while visiting Kitano, a certain person gave this to me. Completed by the Dharma-seeking bhikṣu Jinshū of the Seirinbō Hall at Kanshū-ji Temple; his age is thirty-six.

Now, having revised and collated these forty-eight fascicles of the *Xuanzhuan*, and having verified them against the original rhyme-charts as proof for establishing the fundamental principles and founding the teachings, I have first commissioned the carving of printing blocks.
By this merit, I vow that all beings may equally give rise to the bodhicitta and be reborn in the Land of Peace and Bliss.
